final_proof:
Equip \(\mathbb R^d\) with its usual inner product
\[
\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^d x_k y_k
\]
and the induced Euclidean norm. This makes \(\mathbb R^d\) a Hilbert space: if \((x^{(n)})\) is Cauchy in this norm, then for each \(k\),
\[
|x_k^{(n)}-x_k^{(m)}|\leq \|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|,
\]
so \((x_k^{(n)})\) is Cauchy in \(\mathbb R\). By completeness of \(\mathbb R\), let \(x_k=\lim_{n\to\infty}x_k^{(n)}\), and put \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\). Since the sum has only finitely many terms,
\[
\|x^{(n)}-x\|^2=\sum_{k=1}^d |x_k^{(n)}-x_k|^2\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Thus every Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb R^d\) converges.

For the standard vector \(e_i\), its \(k\)-th coordinate is the Kronecker delta \(\delta_{ik}\). Hence, for \(1\leq i,j\leq d\),
\[
\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^d\delta_{ik}\delta_{jk}=\delta_{ij}.
\]
Therefore \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) form an orthonormal set.

Now let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\in\mathbb R^d\). Equality in every coordinate gives
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^d x_i e_i.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_d\}=\mathbb R^d.
\]
Its closed linear span is therefore also all of \(\mathbb R^d\). Thus \(\{e_1,\ldots,e_d\}\) is a complete orthonormal set, which is precisely a Hilbert-space basis of \(\mathbb R^d\).
